extracted.intended_audience: disability rights advocates, media/regulatory observers, general public interested in broadcasting standards
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations used by Ofcom, broadcasters, and disability/mental-health organisations to judge whether television comedy material (satire/jokes) breaches broadcasting standards, causes harm, or warrants apology/punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting a known individual's disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ofcom found the jokes had a 'straightforward focus on Harvey Price and his disability' and 'appeared to directly target and mock the mental and physical disabilities of a known eight year-old child who had not himself chosen to be in the public eye'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directly targeting and mocking a specific individual's disability — especially a child who did not choose publicity — is a key factor indicating a breach of the broadcasting code and increases the likelihood the material will be judged offensive and inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerable potential to be highly offensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Ofcom said the material 'had considerable potential to be highly offensive to the audience'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The potential to cause strong offence to viewers is explicitly considered by regulators when determining whether content breaches standards, regardless of comedic intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial consideration and signposting as mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ofcom noted the content was 'carefully considered' by senior editorial staff before broadcast, and that the show was clearly signposted by Channel 4 as potentially offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of internal editorial review and clear advance warnings to viewers can mitigate regulatory findings (e.g., avoiding a finding of a 'fundamental' breach) and reduce the likelihood of financial penalties or forced on-air apologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical context and audience understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: In a separate ruling Ofcom said the sketch satirising the Time to Change campaign did not breach the code because the 'intention... to use satire and controversy to make a joke about society’s attitudes to mental health... would have been well understood by the majority of the audience'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When controversial material can be shown to have a clear satirical target (societal attitudes rather than individuals) and is likely to be understood by the audience in that context, regulators may deem it justified and not in breach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume of public complaints as a metric
rubrics_metrics.description: The material led to 500 complaints to Ofcom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The number of complaints is used as an indicator of public reaction and can prompt regulatory review, but high complaint numbers do not automatically result in fines or mandatory apologies — context and other factors still determine outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distress caused to affected communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Rethink and other organisations said the sketch had caused 'distress to a lot of people' and expressed disappointment with Ofcom's ruling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported distress from the communities depicted (or their representative organisations) is an important evaluative consideration; regulators and broadcasters weigh such harm when deciding whether content crossed a line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of regulatory treatment across protected characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argued 'I don’t think they would be as lenient if these issues were related to race,' calling for equivalent standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perceived or actual inconsistencies in how regulators treat offences concerning different protected characteristics (e.g., disability vs race) form part of public and advocacy-group assessments of regulatory fairness and thoroughness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject's lack of choice in public exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Ofcom emphasised the target was 'a known eight year-old child who had not himself chosen to be in the public eye'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether the targeted person voluntarily sought publicity (or is a public figure) influences how acceptable it is to subject them to satire or mockery; targeting those who did not choose public exposure is treated as more problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing freedom of expression against harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Rethink stated: 'Rethink fully supports freedom of expression, but the line must be drawn somewhere.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation involves balancing a broadcaster's/expression rights and satirical aims against potential harm; regulators consider intent and public interest but also whether harm or offense outweighs expressive value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission or acknowledgement of editorial error
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked whether it would apologise and if it agreed with Ofcom’s conclusion that it had made an error of editorial judgement, Channel 4 declined to comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a broadcaster acknowledges editorial mistakes can affect public response and calls for apology; acceptance of fault may influence reputational and regulatory consequences even if formal sanctions are not applied.
